instructions: Closing time of the evening cellar tour. Tomáš counts the last tourists out; Mizuki lingers at a bricked archway nobody mentions. She asks him in broken English whether the wall is old. Under her breath she says in Japanese, in quotation marks, that the wall seems to be breathing, and he understands and pretends he did not.
reply:
The last tourists climbed the stone stairs in a loose line, phone lights bobbing against the damp vault, and Tomáš counted them out the way he counted everything on a tour: heads, then coats, then the iron ring that always made someone reach for it. Eleven. At the top, the door closed with its old weight and the bolt slid home. Nine o'clock, on the nose. He let out a breath and tipped the headlamp down from his forehead, so that its beam swept across the brick, the sweating candle-cups the company kept for effect, and the rough stone of the floor.

Mizuki had not gone up. She stood at the far end of the cellar, where the tour never stopped, in front of the archway that had been bricked up before anyone thought to write down why. Her hands were pushed into the pockets of her grey jacket. He had seen her look at it on the way in, once and quickly, the way she might check a patient's color before she spoke to them, and then she had looked away.

"Tomáš," she said. Her English came slowly, each word set down like a cup on a table. "This wall. Is it old?"

"Older than the house above it," he said, coming down the last steps. "The arch is maybe fourteenth century. The bricks are newer. Somebody closed it up a long time ago, and nobody has ever told us who, or why."

She nodded, though not as if she were satisfied. She lifted her palm and laid it flat against the brick, very lightly, and held it there.

Her lips moved. She murmured in Japanese, so low it was barely sound at all: "It is breathing."

Tomáš stopped with his boot on the last step. The words went into him cleanly, the way they did in the novels he had read by lamplight for four years, and for a moment he was not in the cellar but in some quieter room of his own head, a book open in his hands. He knew exactly what she had said. He also knew she had not meant him to hear it. If he answered her now in Japanese, he would have to explain the late nights, the subtitles, the notebook full of words he never used aloud, and he did not want to explain anything tonight.

He cleared his throat. "Cold wall," he answered in English. "Damp. Very old places can seem to breathe. Air moves through the cracks in the mortar."

She turned her head. In the glow from his forehead lamp, which he had not yet switched off, her face was careful and unreadable, and she did not take her hand from the brick. Somewhere behind the stone, water dripped, once, twice, into a space that nobody had measured.

instructions: Mizuki wakes face down in wet reeds under a huge moon. Cold, no cellar, no tour. She finds Tomáš unconscious; he comes round and they talk in broken English. She says in Japanese, afraid, in quotation marks, where they are; he does not react to the Japanese and answers in English, careful. He never says or implies that he does not understand Japanese (he does; from her point of view he just replies in English without reacting).
reply:
The cold woke her before anything else did. It came up through her cheek, through the sleeve of her grey jacket, through the wet earth soaking her knees. Mizuki lay still and let her eyes open on a blur of black-green stalks, each one taller than her head, bending in a wind she could not feel on her face.

She pushed up onto her palms. Reeds sprang back against her arms and dripped down her wrists. The ground gave under her hands like something that had only just decided to hold. Above the reeds hung a moon so large and low that it seemed to rest on the stalks, pale and swollen, and its light lay across black water that stretched away in every direction she turned.

There was no arch. No cellar, no iron ring, no candle-cups sweating on the brick. Her mind tried to put the stone stairs back under her and failed. Her fingers found mud, then a root, then cloth.

"Tomáš," she said in Japanese, and her voice came out thin. "Tomáš. Where are we?"

He lay face down a few steps away, one arm flung over a tussock as if he had tried to catch something on the way down. His hair was full of mud. His headlamp had fallen beside his head, and its beam burned straight across the water, lighting a narrow path of ripples she could not explain.

She crawled to him and turned him over. His eyes were shut. For one terrible moment she felt nothing at his neck, and then she felt it, a slow, stubborn beat. She let out a breath she had not known she was holding and pressed her palm flat against his chest, the way she would have checked a patient, counting.

His eyelids moved. He groaned and coughed water onto the reeds.

"Easy," she said in broken English. "Easy. You fall. Maybe hit head."

He blinked at the moon, then at her, then past her shoulder at the endless flat dark. "Mizuki," he answered in English, carefully, as though each word had to be tested before he trusted it with his weight. "Where is this?"

"I do not know." Her voice shook and she hated it. "Not cellar. Not Prague, I think. Water. Only water."

He pushed himself up slowly, one hand sunk in the mud, and took in the distance with one long, measuring look. "Okay," he said. "We stay together. We do not walk into the water."

She nodded. Her hand had closed on his sleeve, and she did not let go.

instructions: Tomáš takes stock; they still speak English, hers broken: phone 58 percent and no signal, headlamp, notebook, a water bottle; her bag, a first-aid kit, a phone. He thinks in Czech, swears in Czech, decides to follow the river downstream. He still hides that he understood her mutter.
reply:
He sat up slowly and made himself count things, the way he counted a tour group at the top of the stairs. Hands: two, scraped raw across the palms, the left one bleeding into the mud. Legs: both working, though his right knee had already begun to ache. Headlamp: lying in the reeds where it had fallen, its beam still burning across the water. He picked it up. The glass was cracked corner to corner, but when he thumbed the switch the light came on, dim and yellow, and he let out a breath he had not known he was holding.

His phone was in the inside pocket of his coat. He pressed the side button. The screen woke at fifty-eight percent, and above the battery the signal bars stood empty. He turned the phone over in his hands, as if the back of it might explain itself.

"Fifty-eight," he said. "No signal. Nothing."

Mizuki knelt beside him with her knees sunk in the mud. Her own phone lay in her palm, its black glass dark. She pressed the button anyway, twice, then set it down on a tussock without a word.

He went on counting. The notebook was still in his breast pocket. He drew it out, and the cover was soaked, but the pages held. In one corner the ink had run, and a column of his Japanese words had bled blue into the paper. He closed it carefully and put it back. The water bottle was clipped to his belt, half full.

Mizuki had her bag over one shoulder, the strap wound tight around her wrist. She unzipped it and lifted out a grey plastic case with a red cross on the lid, then a packet of wet tissues, then a small roll of bandage. She held the bandage up to the headlamp as if checking it for holes.

"Bag is okay," she said. "I have bandage. Medicine, little. Enough for one day, maybe."

"Good. That is good." He pressed the heel of his hand against his forehead and swore under his breath, in Czech, long and low, and the reeds swallowed the sound.

She looked at him. "Bad word?"

"Very bad word," he said in English. "My mother would be angry."

Something moved at the corner of her mouth, not quite a smile. She began to wind the bandage around her own hand, pulling it tight with her teeth.

He turned the headlamp toward the water. Upstream, the moon lay broken on the surface, and the reeds closed in on both banks like a crowd that did not want to be looked at. Downstream the channel curved away into darker growth, but the current moved that way, slow and steady, pulling the scum of the flood with it. Every river went somewhere. Rivers did not run in circles, whatever else this place did.

"We follow the river," he said. "Downstream. Slowly. We keep the water on our left, and we do not go into it."

Mizuki finished the knot and looked at the dark channel for a long moment. Then she stood, swaying a little, and gripped his sleeve again. "Which way is the bank?" she asked. "I cannot see."

He pointed with the headlamp, the beam trembling across the reeds, and did not tell her that he had understood every word she had muttered at the bricked arch.

instructions: She slips and says in Japanese that she wants to go home; he answers in Japanese before he can stop himself. Her shock, his embarrassment, their first real conversation. Her Japanese is natural, his stiff and bookish.
reply:
The mud gave way under her left foot, and she went down to one knee in a hidden hollow. Cold water soaked through her trousers to the thigh. Her hand shot out and closed on Tomáš's sleeve, and she hung on, breathing hard, while the words spilled out before she could stop them.

"I want to go home," she said in Japanese. Her voice cracked on the last word. "I want my bed, my kitchen, my brother on the phone on Sunday. I want a phone that works."

Tomáš had been reaching for the headlamp. His hand stopped in the air above it.

"I want to go home," he answered in Japanese, and then his face changed, as though he had heard himself from outside.

The words were right, but the way he said them was wrong. Each syllable came out squared off and careful, too polite, the way a textbook would address a guest at a formal dinner. He sounded like someone reading aloud from a page he had memorized in a quiet room. It was so stiff that for one moment she almost laughed, and then she did not, because she understood what it meant.

She stared at him. The headlamp's beam slid off his face and across the black water. In the cellar he had answered her in English. He had said the wall was cold and damp, that old places only seemed to breathe. He had been looking at her the whole time, she realized, waiting to see whether she would speak again.

"You understand," she said in Japanese. It was not a question.

He winced, and his ears went red beneath the mud. He looked down at his scraped palms as if they might offer him a better answer. "Yes," he said. "Since the cellar. I am sorry. I did not want to explain."

"Explain what?"

"That I have read too many novels." He pressed his wounded hand against his knee. "Four years. Subtitles, late at night, a notebook full of words I never say out loud. It is embarrassing. My Japanese is like an old book. Very correct. Very useless in a conversation."

Her grip on his sleeve did not loosen. Something in her chest, tight since the arch, gave way a little, and she heard herself answer without deciding to. "Your Japanese is not useless. It is strange. You say 'please' like you are apologizing to the furniture."

He let out a short, startled breath that was almost a laugh. The reeds leaned toward them with the wind, and a long ripple ran out across the water and died against the bank.

"Then teach me," he said in Japanese. "Properly. Tell me how a Japanese person would say what you just said."

She looked at the dark channel, then at his face, and for the first time since the stairs she did not feel that she was alone in the reeds.

instructions: Walking along the bank. He explains, too eagerly, what an isekai is, looks for a status window and a summoner, finds none. She teases his stiff speech, asks where he learned it, and he is embarrassed. She decides what to do first: water, shelter, find people.
reply:
They walked the bank with the water on their left, the reeds whispering against their shoulders. The mud sucked at each step. Every few paces Tomáš swung the headlamp toward the ground to find firm tussock before he trusted it with her weight.

"In the novels," he said in Japanese, then stopped, because she had already turned her head. He swallowed and started again, faster now, the words tumbling out before he could square them. "In the novels there is always a moment like this. A person from our world wakes up somewhere else, and the first thing they look for is a window. A status window. It shows the level, the strength, the skills. It floats in the air, like a screen."

"Screen," she repeated, flat.

"Yes. Like a screen. And there is always a summoner, an old man in robes, who says you were called here for a reason." He lifted one hand toward the moon and moved his fingers in the air, a small, hopeful gesture. "Status. Show me status."

Nothing answered him but the wind and a splash somewhere in the reeds.

Mizuki watched his hand fall back to his side. Her mouth twitched, and for a moment the tiredness on her face gave way to something close to her old teasing. "Your hand is very bad at magic."

He winced. "I know."

"And your Japanese." She tilted her head and studied him in the thin yellow beam. "Where did you learn it? From what? Books for old men? You say 'please' like you are asking a judge for mercy."

His ears burned again. He looked at the cracked glass of the headlamp instead of at her. "Novels. Subtitles. I told you."

"Hm." She let it go, but he saw the corner of her mouth stay curved.

She stopped. The reeds parted around her, and she turned in a slow circle, reading the flat black distance the way she might read a ward at night, checking each bed in turn. The moon had climbed a finger's width. Its light lay on the water in a long, broken road.

"Water first," she said. "We drink only what is clean, or we boil it, if we can make a fire. Then shelter, a place out of the wind. Then people. Rivers have villages beside them. Someone walks along the water, so we walk too."

She took the first step along the bank, and her hand found his sleeve again, and he followed her with the lamp pointed at the path ahead.

instructions: Dusk and cold. Mizuki, a nurse, organises: checks his head, rations the water, builds a windbreak from reeds. A smell of wood smoke; a lantern on the river. They argue softly in Japanese about whether to call out.
reply:
The light went out of the sky all at once, the way it did on the ward when someone pulled the blinds, and the cold rose off the water to fill the gap. Mizuki knelt in the reeds and drew her grey jacket tighter. Her breath hung in front of her face.

"Sit," she said in Japanese. "Face the light. Look at me."

Tomáš obeyed, lowering himself onto a tussock with the headlamp balanced on his knee. She took his jaw in both hands and turned his head toward the beam. His pupils were wide and black in the yellow glow. She moved the light left, then right, and watched both pupils close at the same speed.

"Head," she said in broken English. "Hurt?"

"Yes." He touched the back of his skull and winced. "Here. Big bump. Stupid."

Her fingers moved through his hair, parting the mud, feeling for the swelling beneath the skin. No blood on her fingertips. She counted his breaths without meaning to, the way she had counted a thousand breaths on night shift. "You sleep tonight, I wake you every hour. Every hour, you say your name. Understand?"

"Every hour. Name. Okay." He tried a small smile. "Very bad hospital."

"Very bad patient."

She counted the water next. The bottle at his belt, half full. Her own, a third of that. She set them side by side on the reeds like instruments on a tray and did the sums in her head. A few sips at dusk, a few at dawn, nothing wasted. Then she turned back to the reeds.

The stalks were thick and dry at the base, where the wind had not reached them. She pulled armfuls, snapping them, and laid them in a tangle on the lee side of a low hummock, pressing the tops down into the mud until they held. Tomáš worked beside her with his bleeding hand wrapped in a strip torn from his scarf. Slowly a wall rose, knee-high, then waist-high, shielding a hollow where the wind could not reach.

Then the smell came across the water: wood smoke, thin and sweet, drifting low over the reeds.

Mizuki froze with a bundle in her arms. Tomáš lifted his head.

Out on the channel, a small yellow light hung above the black surface, swaying with the current. A lantern, perhaps, or a fire on a boat. It did not come nearer. It did not go away.

"We call," Tomáš said in Japanese, very quietly, each word placed with care. "Maybe they hear us."

"No." She set the reeds down slowly. "We do not know who they are. Maybe they are not kind."

"Maybe they have fire. Maybe they have a doctor."

"You do not know that." Her voice came out harder than she meant. "We wait. We watch."

He looked at the light, then at her, and she saw him open his mouth to argue. Then he closed it again.
